title: Die Geschichte von den schwarzen Buben
titleEn: The Story of the Blackened Boys
source: Heinrich Hoffmann, Der Struwwelpeter, Rütten & Loening, Frankfurt am Main, 564. Auflage — the canonical later text in modernized spelling (via Project Gutenberg #24571). Fresh Lectorium translation from the German.
about: One of Heinrich Hoffmann’s 1845 cautionary verses, and the one that has aged worst: three boys jeer at a Black passer-by walking under his parasol, and great Nikolas dips them in his inkstand until they come out blacker than the person they laughed at. The poem never settles whether that person is a man or a child — it calls him »Mohr«, then »Mohrchen« and »Mohrenkind« — and the translation follows it. It trades on a racial caricature of its period — »Mohr« was the ordinary German word in 1845 and is offensive in German and English alike today, and the illustration is a caricature. Lectorium presents the piece unaltered, as the historical document it is, with the notes saying plainly what the words meant then; Hoffmann’s target is the mocking boys, whose punishment is the whole story, but the terms he reaches for are his century’s and not ours.

advisory.lede: This poem contains a racial caricature of its period, including a word that is now a slur.
advisory.more: Hoffmann’s 1845 verse opens on »ein kohlpechrabenschwarzer Mohr« — a Black passer-by described with a word that was ordinary German then and is offensive in German and English alike now. Three boys jeer at him and are dipped in ink for it. Lectorium presents the poem unaltered, as the historical document it is; Hoffmann’s target is the mocking boys, whose punishment is the whole story, but the terms he reaches for are his century’s.

sentences.t:
Es ging spazieren vor dem Tor
ein kohlpechrabenschwarzer Mohr.
sentences.l:
There went walking before the gate
a coal-pitch-raven-black Moor.
sentences.i:
Out beyond the town gate there went walking
a Moor, black as coal and pitch and raven.
sentences.n: »Mohr« was in 1845 the everyday German word for a Black person — from Latin »Maurus«, but with none of the narrower sense English ‘Moor’ can carry; it was simply the word a nursery book reached for. It is offensive in German today, as its English counterpart is, and Lectorium keeps it because softening it would hide what this poem is. On the grammar: »Es ging …« puts a placeholder »es« in the front slot so that the subject can arrive last, at the rhyme (the same trick as »es brennt die Hand«). »vor dem Tor« is outside the town gate — Frankfurt still had its gates, and the walk beyond them was the ordinary promenade. »kohlpechrabenschwarz« stacks three black things — coal, pitch, raven — into one word.

sentences.t:
Die Sonne schien ihm aufs Gehirn,
da nahm er seinen Sonnenschirm.
sentences.l:
The sun shone him onto-the brain,
there took he his sun-shade.
sentences.i:
The sun beat down on his head,
so he took his parasol.
sentences.n: »ihm … aufs Gehirn« — the dative of the person plus the definite article, where English wants ‘on his head’ (the same pattern as the dog biting Friederich »ins Bein«). »das Gehirn« is literally the brain: comic overstatement, chosen to rhyme with »Sonnenschirm«, the parasol, which a gentleman carried in summer.

sentences.t:
Da kam der Ludwig hergerannt
und trug sein Fähnchen in der Hand.
sentences.l:
There came the Ludwig running-hither
and carried his little-flag in the hand.
sentences.i:
Then along came Ludwig at a run,
carrying his little flag in his hand.
sentences.n: »herrennen« — ‘to come running’; the »her-« always means motion toward where the speaker stands. »das Fähnchen« is the -chen diminutive of »Fahne«: a toy flag on a stick. Each of the three boys arrives carrying his plaything, and each plaything turns up again in the pictures.

sentences.t:
Der Kaspar kam mit schnellem Schritt
und brachte seine Brezel mit.
sentences.l:
The Kaspar came with swift step
and brought his pretzel along.
sentences.i:
Kaspar came at a smart pace,
bringing his pretzel with him.
sentences.n: »mitbringen« is separable: »brachte … mit«, with the »mit« waiting at the line’s end (the dog carried the whip home the same way). »die Brezel« — the pretzel, the German street snack then as now, and a child’s outing food.

sentences.t:
Und auch der Wilhelm war nicht steif
und brachte seinen runden Reif.
sentences.l:
And also the Wilhelm was not stiff
and brought his round hoop.
sentences.i:
And Wilhelm too was not one to hang back,
and brought his round hoop.
sentences.n: »steif« is literally ‘stiff’, here in the social sense — stand-offish, holding aloof; »war nicht steif« = ‘didn’t hang back either.’ »der Reif« is the hoop a child drove along the street with a stick, the standard 19th-century toy — and it rhymes with »steif«, which is plainly why the line says what it says.

sentences.t:
Die schrien und lachten alle drei,
als dort das Mohrchen ging vorbei,
weil es so schwarz wie Tinte sei!
sentences.l:
They shrieked and laughed all three,
when there the little-Moor went past,
because it so black as ink were!
sentences.i:
All three shrieked and laughed
as the little Moor went past,
because — so they said — he was as black as ink!
sentences.n: »vorbeigehen« is separable: »ging … vorbei«. »das Mohrchen« is the -chen diminutive, and since every -chen word is neuter, the poem refers to a person as »es« — grammar rather than contempt, though English can only say ‘he.’ And »sei« is the subjunctive of reported speech: the reason is given in the boys’ voice, not the narrator’s — ‘because (they said) he was as black as ink.’ German marks borrowed claims this way constantly, and it is worth watching for: the subjunctive is the narrator declining to vouch for what is said.

sentences.t:
Da kam der große Nikolas
mit seinem großen Tintenfaß.
sentences.l:
There came the big Nikolas
with his big ink-well.
sentences.i:
Then came great Nikolas
with his great inkstand.
sentences.n: »das Tintenfaß« is the inkwell — in the 1840s a household wrote with a dipped pen, and the ink stood in a stoneware pot; here it is man-sized. »groß« twice over, for the man and for the pot. »Faß« is the pre-reform spelling of »Fass«. The name shifts between »Nikolas« and »Niklas« as the meter wants; readers have long heard St. Nicholas behind it, the figure who comes to judge children, though the poem never says so.

sentences.t:
Der sprach: »Ihr Kinder, hört mir zu
und laßt den Mohren hübsch in Ruh!
sentences.l:
He spoke: “You children, hear to me
and leave the Moor nicely in peace!
sentences.i:
He said: “Now children, listen to me,
and leave the Moor in peace!
sentences.n: »der« is the demonstrative pronoun standing for ‘he’. »zuhören« is separable and takes the dative: »hört mir zu« = ‘listen to me.’ »in Ruhe lassen« = ‘to leave alone’, with »Ruh« clipped. »hübsch« adverbial once more — ‘properly, kindly now’, as in »hübsch ordentlich«. »den Mohren« carries the -n of the weak masculine declension.

sentences.t:
Was kann denn dieser Mohr dafür,
daß er so weiß nicht ist wie ihr?«
sentences.l:
What can then this Moor for-it,
that he so white not is as you?”
sentences.i:
How is this Moor to blame
for not being as white as you are?”
sentences.n: »Was kann er dafür?« is an idiom that will not go across word for word: ‘what can he do about it?’, i.e. ‘how is it his fault?’ The »da-« of »dafür« points forward to the »daß«-clause that follows — German often plants such a pronoun first and explains it after. »denn« in a question is the untranslatable softener, roughly ‘well, then.’ The argument is the poem’s moral, and it is aimed at the boys.

sentences.t:
Die Buben aber folgten nicht
und lachten ihm ins Angesicht
und lachten ärger als zuvor
über den armen, schwarzen Mohr.
sentences.l:
The boys however obeyed not
and laughed him into-the face
and laughed worse than before
over the poor, black Moor.
sentences.i:
But the boys did not obey,
and laughed in his face,
and laughed worse than before
at the poor black Moor.
sentences.n: »folgen« in its older sense ‘to obey’ (it takes the dative). »ihm ins Angesicht lachen« — dative person plus »in das Angesicht«: ‘to laugh in his face’; »Angesicht« is the elevated old word for »Gesicht«. »über jemanden lachen« = ‘to laugh at someone.’ »ärger« is the comparative of »arg«, Friederich’s adjective — ‘worse.’ Three »und«s in four lines pile the offence up until it topples.

sentences.t:
Der Niklas wurde bös und wild,
du siehst es hier auf diesem Bild!
sentences.l:
The Niklas became angry and wild,
you see it here on this picture!
sentences.i:
Niklas grew angry and fierce —
you can see it here in the picture!
sentences.n: »bös« is »böse« clipped, and here it means ‘angry’ rather than ‘wicked’ — one word does both jobs in German. »werden« plus an adjective = ‘to become.’ And the narrator turns to the reader and points at the illustration, as he did over Paulinchen’s burning match: the pictures are part of the text, not decoration.

sentences.t:
Er packte gleich die Buben fest,
beim Arm, beim Kopf, beim Rock und West
den Wilhelm und den Ludewig,
den Kaspar auch, der wehrte sich.
sentences.l:
He seized at once the boys tight,
by-the arm, by-the head, by-the coat and waistcoat,
the Wilhelm and the Ludewig,
the Kaspar too, he defended himself.
sentences.i:
He seized the boys at once and held them fast —
by the arm, by the head, by coat and waistcoat —
Wilhelm and Ludewig,
and Kaspar too — he fought back.
sentences.n: »festpacken« is separable: »packte … fest« = ‘grabbed and held fast.’ »beim Arm« = »bei dem Arm« — German takes hold of you ‘by the arm’ with the definite article and no possessive. »West« is »Weste« clipped, the waistcoat. »Ludewig« is the older, longer spelling of »Ludwig«, worth a syllable to the meter. »sich wehren« = ‘to defend oneself, resist’. »der wehrte sich« only looks like a relative clause: the verb stands second, not last, so this is a fresh main clause and »der« is the demonstrative pronoun, ‘that one’ — ‘he fought back.’ A relative would have read »der sich wehrte«, with the verb at the end.

sentences.t:
Er tunkt sie in die Tinte tief,
wie auch der Kaspar »Feuer« rief.
sentences.l:
He dips them into the ink deep,
however also the Kaspar “fire” cried.
sentences.i:
He dips them deep into the ink,
for all that Kaspar cried “Fire!”
sentences.n: »wie auch« here is concessive — ‘however much, for all that’, not ‘as also’. Kaspar shouts »Feuer!« because that was the one cry that brought a whole street out of doors; it is the loudest word a child knew, and it does him no good. Note the tense slipping into the present for the deed itself (»tunkt«), as this book does whenever it wants you to watch.

sentences.t:
Bis übern Kopf ins Tintenfaß
tunkt sie der große Nikolas.
sentences.l:
Till over-the head into-the ink-well
dips them the big Nikolas.
sentences.i:
Right over their heads into the inkstand
great Nikolas dips them.
sentences.n: »übern« = »über den«, »ins« = »in das«: verse runs its small words together. The whole direction is fronted so that the verb can stand second and the doer arrive last of all, at the rhyme — German holds a subject back like this whenever it wants the name to land.

sentences.t:
Du siehst sie hier, wie schwarz sie sind,
viel schwärzer als das Mohrenkind.
sentences.l:
You see them here, how black they are,
much blacker than the Moor-child.
sentences.i:
You can see them here, how black they are,
far blacker than the Moor child.
sentences.n: »das Mohrenkind« — the third name the poem gives him, after »Mohr« and »Mohrchen«. The punishment is measured against the person mocked: the boys end blacker than the child they laughed at, and the picture is the argument.

sentences.t:
Der Mohr voraus im Sonnenschein,
die Tintenbuben hinterdrein;
sentences.l:
The Moor ahead in the sunshine,
the ink-boys behind-after;
sentences.i:
The Moor in front in the sunshine,
the ink-boys trailing behind;
sentences.n: Two lines with no verb in them at all — captions rather than sentences, the same verbless snapshot as »wupp! den Daumen in den Mund«. »hinterdrein« = ‘along behind’, an old form of »hinterher«. »die Tintenbuben« is a compound coined on the spot: ink-boys.

sentences.t:
und hätten sie nicht so gelacht,
hätt Niklas sie nicht schwarz gemacht.
sentences.l:
and had they not so laughed,
had Niklas them not black made.
sentences.i:
and if they had not laughed so,
Niklas would not have made them black.
sentences.n: A conditional with no »wenn« in it: German may drop the ‘if’ and put the verb first instead — »hätten sie nicht gelacht« = ‘if they had not laughed.’ Both halves stand in the past subjunctive (»hätten«, and »hätt« for »hätte«), which is how German says ‘would have.’ The moral arrives as a condition rather than a command: it was the mockery, not the child, that fetched the ink.
